slides.title: Single Server Setup
content: A single server setup runs the web application, database, and services on one machine
It is the simplest architecture and is commonly used for MVPs or early-stage applications
It introduces a Single Point of Failure (SPOF), meaning if the server crashes the entire system goes down
Suitable only for low traffic systems due to limited scalability and reliability

slides.title: Web Tier vs Data Tier
content: Separates the application layer (web tier) from the storage layer (data tier)
Web tier handles HTTP requests, business logic, and authentication
Data tier manages databases such as SQL or NoSQL for persistent storage
Improves modularity and allows independent scaling but database can still become a bottleneck

slides.title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
content: Vertical scaling increases resources of a single machine like CPU, RAM, or storage
Horizontal scaling distributes load across multiple machines or servers
Vertical scaling is simple but limited by hardware constraints
Horizontal scaling provides better scalability and fault tolerance for large systems

slides.title: Load Balancer
content: Distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers to avoid overload
Acts as an entry point between clients and backend servers
Uses health checks to route traffic only to healthy servers
Improves availability and reliability by redirecting traffic if a server fails

slides.title: Database Replication
content: Replicates data across multiple database servers using primary-replica architecture
Primary database handles write operations while replicas handle read operations
Improves read scalability and availability
Primary database can still become a bottleneck for heavy write workloads

slides.title: Cache
content: Cache is a fast in-memory storage used to store frequently accessed data
Reduces database load and improves response time
System checks cache first before querying the database
Uses strategies like LRU eviction and TTL expiration for data management

slides.title: Content Delivery Network (CDN)
content: A CDN is a distributed network of servers that cache static content
Stores assets like images, CSS, JavaScript, and videos
Delivers content from servers closer to users to reduce latency
Reduces load on the origin server and improves performance

slides.title: Stateless Web Tier
content: Stateless systems do not store session data on individual servers
Session data is stored in shared storage like Redis or databases
Allows any server to handle any request
Enables easy horizontal scaling and auto-scaling

slides.title: Multi Data Center and GeoDNS
content: Deploys system across multiple geographic data centers
GeoDNS routes users to the nearest or healthiest data center
Improves latency, availability, and disaster recovery
Requires handling data consistency challenges across regions

slides.title: Message Queue
content: Enables asynchronous communication between services
Producers send tasks to the queue and consumers process them later
Helps decouple system components and improve scalability
Prevents slow operations from blocking user requests

slides.title: Logging Metrics and Automation
content: Logging records system events and errors for debugging
Metrics track performance indicators like latency, CPU, and memory usage
Helps monitor system health and detect issues early
Automation supports CI/CD pipelines and auto-scaling in large systems

slides.title: Database Sharding
content: Sharding splits a large database into smaller partitions called shards
Each shard stores a subset of data based on a sharding key
Improves scalability and performance for large datasets
Introduces challenges like shard rebalancing, hotspots, and cross-shard queries
